entry: Individuals and organizations that earn money from songs, recordings, sheet music and concerts. The industry includes songwriters, performers, record labels, music publishers, recording studios, music venues, promoters and performance-rights organizations, as well as managers, lawyers, critics and teachers. The modern Western industry emerged between the 1930s and 1950s, when records replaced sheet music as the most important product. By the 2020s, four major corporate labels, [[Universal Music Group]], [[Sony]] Music Group, Warner Music Group and BMG Rights Management, controlled a majority of the market. Since 2000, sales of recorded music have dropped substantially while live music has grown in importance. Since 2011, streaming has generated more revenue per year than digital downloads, with [[Spotify]], Apple Music and Amazon Music the largest services by subscribers. Global recorded music revenues reached US$29.6 billion in 2024, a 4.8% increase and the tenth consecutive year of growth. Payments to artists per stream remain a continuing source of dispute.

Diverse musical traditions of the African continent, shaped by distinct regional and national cultures. African music is highly rhythmic and often uses polyrhythm, in which one rhythm is played against another. Percussion is central, and sub-Saharan traditions rely on [[Xylophone|xylophones]], [[Djembe|djembes]], [[Drum|drums]] and tone-producing instruments such as the mbira. Call-and-response singing and improvisation over a core rhythmic pattern are common. Much traditional music is passed down through [[Oral tradition|oral tradition]] and is integral to communal, religious and social life. Genres include highlife, mbube, jùjú, afrobeat, mbalax and soukous. Music of the African diaspora, including American genres such as [[Blues|blues]] and [[Jazz|jazz]], was shaped to varying degrees by African traditions, and Latin American genres such as [[Samba|samba]] developed from the music of enslaved Africans. These genres have in turn influenced contemporary African popular music.

Traditions of music in China, including classical court forms, folk music and modern popular music. Archaeological finds show a developed musical culture as early as the [[Zhou dynasty]] (1122–257 BC), when a formal system of court and ceremonial music later termed yayue was established. Bone [[Flute|flutes]] dated to 9,000 years ago have been found at Jiahu Village in Henan. Traditional forms emphasize pentatonic scales, and in the Zhou dynasty music was conceived as a cosmological manifestation of nature, integrated into the order of [[Yin and yang|yin and yang]]. [[Confucius]] held that correct music cultivated the individual and that formal court music was morally uplifting, while Mozi condemned music in *Against Music* as an extravagance. In ancient China, musicians had lower social status than painters. Since the early 20th century, Chinese composers have integrated Western orchestration and notation, and popular genres now draw on global markets, though state oversight shapes lyrical content.

Study of the theoretical frameworks for understanding the practices and possibilities of music. The term has three related uses: the rudiments needed to read notation, such as key signatures, time signatures and rhythmic notation; the study of scholars' views on music from antiquity to the present; and a subtopic of [[Musicology|musicology]] that seeks to define processes and general principles in music. Music theory covers tuning systems, [[Scale (music)|scales]], consonance and dissonance, and rhythmic relationships, as well as [[Harmony|harmony]] and [[Counterpoint|counterpoint]]. As a practical discipline it includes the methods composers and performers use in creating and performing music, such as orchestration, ornamentation and improvisation. Guido Adler, one of the founders of musicology, wrote that "the science of music originated at the same time as the art of sounds." Teaching as a tenure-track music theorist at a university in the United States or Canada typically requires graduate study to the MA or PhD level.

Video that integrates a song or album with imagery produced for promotional or artistic purposes. Modern music videos are primarily a marketing device intended to promote the sale of recordings and are shown on music television and streaming sites such as [[YouTube]]. Precursors include the illustrated song of 1894, in which a magic lantern projected still images during live performances, and the musical short films that followed the arrival of recorded sound in theaters in the 1920s. Promotional videos became popular in the 1960s, and the format rose to prominence in the 1980s when [[MTV]] based its channel around the medium. Styles range from animation and live action to documentary and abstract film. [[Michael Jackson]]'s 14-minute video for *Thriller* (1983) set benchmarks for production scale and commercial impact. [[Madonna]]'s 1985 video for "Material Girl" imitated the style of 1930s–50s Hollywood musicals.

System of symbols for representing music visually, recording the elements considered important for performance in a given tradition. Ancient cultures used symbols for melodies and rhythms, but none was particularly comprehensive. The earliest known notation is a [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]] tablet from Nippur in [[Babylonia]], dating to about 1400 BCE. The direct ancestor of the modern Western system emerged in medieval Europe, where it was developed to standardize the performance of plainsong melodies. Notation developed further during the Renaissance and [[Baroque]] periods and continued to evolve with instrumental technology in the Classical and Romantic eras. Since the 20th century some composers have used graphical notation, and computer-based scorewriter programs have been used since the 1980s. Classical performers mostly use staves, time signatures, key signatures and noteheads, the Nashville Number System is the main method in professional country music, and [[Guitar|guitar]] players often use tablature. Notation has been written on stone, clay tablets, [[Papyrus|papyrus]] and [[Parchment|parchment]], and later printed.

Form of theatrical performance that combines songs, spoken dialogue, acting and dance. The story and emotional content are conveyed through words, music, movement and technical elements as an integrated whole, and the music is given equal importance to the dialogue. Since the early 20th century such stage works have generally been called musicals. Modern Western musical theatre emerged in the 19th century, with structural elements established by the light operas of Jacques Offenbach in France and [[Gilbert and Sullivan]] in Britain. Edwardian musical comedies and the Princess Theatre musicals (1915–1918) followed, leading to *Show Boat* (1927) and *Oklahoma!* (1943). Later landmarks include *My Fair Lady* (1956), *Les Misérables* (1985), *The Phantom of the Opera* (1986) and *Hamilton* (2015). Most musicals run from one and a half to three hours. They are staged on Broadway and in London's West End, off-Broadway, in regional and community theatres, and on tour.

Person who composes, conducts or performs music, especially instrumental music. According to the United States Employment Service, the term designates a person who follows music as a profession. Musicians include songwriters, who write both music and lyrics; conductors, who direct a performance; and performers, who are singers or [[Musical instrument|instrumentalists]]. A musician may perform alone or as part of a group, band or [[Orchestra|orchestra]], and many perform across several genres. A musician who records and releases music is often called a recording artist, while one who writes art music, soundtracks or [[Classical music|classical]] music is usually called a composer. Conductors lead an ensemble, typically an orchestra or [[Choir|choral]] group, through gestures and eye contact. A music producer, though not a musician outright, oversees the recording process and the creative direction of an album or song.

Academic, research-based study of music, as distinct from composition or performance. Musicology draws on fields including [[Psychology|psychology]], [[Sociology|sociology]], [[Acoustics|acoustics]], neurology, the natural sciences and computer science. It is traditionally divided into three branches. Historical musicology studies the history of musical traditions, the origins of works and the lives of composers. Ethnomusicology draws on anthropology, particularly [[Field research|field research]], to understand how and why people make music. Systematic musicology includes [[Music theory|music theory]], aesthetics, pedagogy, musical acoustics and organology, the study of instruments. Cognitive musicology models the mental processes involved in music, and computational musicology uses computers in research. Music therapy is a specialized form of applied musicology. Formal musicology education was re-established in German and Austrian universities in the 19th century.

Smoothbore, muzzle-loaded long gun that used black powder. It appeared in the early 16th century as a heavier variant of the [[Arquebus|arquebus]], capable of penetrating [[Plate armour|plate armor]]. The first recorded use of the term came in 1499. As heavy armor declined, this form gradually disappeared by the mid-16th century, but musketeers remained the generic term for smoothbore long guns until the mid-19th century. [[Bayonet|Bayonets]] were attached to muskets in several parts of the world from the late 16th to 17th centuries. Breech-loading firearms with self-contained cartridges, introduced by Casimir Lefaucheux in 1835, began to make muskets obsolete. Rifled muskets using the Minié ball, invented by Claude-Étienne Minié in 1849, became common, and the first reliable repeating rifles, the 1860 Henry rifle and its 1866 descendant the Winchester rifle, superseded muskets entirely.

Hoofed mammal of the family [[Bovidae]] native to the Arctic, noted for its thick coat and for the strong odor males emit during the seasonal rut, from which its name derives. Its Inuktitut name, umingmak, translates to "the bearded one." Despite its name, the muskox is more closely related to [[Sheep|sheep]] and [[Goat|goats]] than to oxen, and it is placed in its own genus, *Ovibos*, Latin for "sheep-ox." Bulls weigh 600–800 pounds (270–360 kg) and have long, shaggy coats with a dense underwool. Muskoxen are found mainly in [[Greenland]], the Canadian Arctic territories of the Northwest Territories and [[Nunavut]], and [[Alaska]]. They were formerly present in Eurasia, where the youngest natural records date to around 2,700 years ago. Reintroduced populations live in Alaska, [[Yukon]] and Siberia, and an introduced population in [[Norway]] has partly spread to [[Sweden]]. When threatened, the herd forms a circle with horns facing outward to protect calves from predators.

Medium-sized semiaquatic [[Rodent|rodent]] native to North America and the only living species in the genus *Ondatra*. Adults weigh 0.6–2 kg (1¼–4½ lb) and measure 20–35 cm (8–14 in) in body length, excluding the tail. Their short, thick fur is medium to dark brown, and their scaly tails are laterally compressed and mainly help with directional stability in the water. Webbed hind feet provide most of their propulsion, and they can swim underwater for 12 to 17 minutes. Muskrats live in families of a male and female pair and their young. They build nests in banks with underwater entrances, and in marshes they construct mounds called push-ups, up to 90 cm (3 ft) high, from vegetation and mud. They feed mostly on cattails and other aquatic vegetation and occasionally on small animals. The muskrat is the largest species in the subfamily Arvicolinae, which includes mostly [[Vole|voles]] and [[Lemming|lemmings]]. It has been introduced to parts of Eurasia and South America, and it is a source of food and fur for people.

Transnational Sunni Islamist organization founded in [[Egypt]] in 1928 by the schoolteacher and imam Hassan al-Banna. Its stated aim is a state ruled by [[Sharia]] under a [[Caliphate|caliphate]], and it combines political activism with Islamic charity work. The Arab Spring brought the group legalization and political power in Egypt, where its candidate, Mohamed Morsi, won the 2012 presidential election. Morsi was overthrown in 2013, and the group was then banned in Egypt. The thinker [[Sayyid Qutb]] promoted takfirism in his 1964 book *Milestones*, a doctrine that continues to inspire many jihadist movements. The group abandoned violence in the 1970s. Several governments, including those of [[Saudi Arabia]] and the United States, designate its flagship group or specific chapters as terrorist organizations.

Arab conquest of the [[Sasanian Empire]] by the [[Rashidun Caliphate]] between 633 and 651 CE, as part of the early Muslim conquests. The Sasanian state was weakened by the Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628 and by a civil war that followed the execution of Khosrow II in 628. The first Rashidun invasion, in 633, took parts of Asoristan, the Sasanian center in Mesopotamia. A second invasion began in 636, and a decisive victory at the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah ended Sasanian control west of modern Iran. For six years the [[Zagros Mountains]] marked the boundary. In 642 the caliph [[Umar]] ordered a full-scale invasion of the rest of the empire. By 651 most urban centers in Iranian lands had come under Muslim domination, except provinces along the [[Caspian Sea]], though many cities rebelled before reinforcements suppressed the uprisings. Islamization was gradual over centuries, and [[Zoroastrianism]] declined. Iran remained mostly Sunni until the Safavids converted it to Shia Islam in the 16th century.

headword: Muslim conquests in the Indian subcontinent
sort_key: muslim conquests in the indian subcontinent
entry: Series of military campaigns and territorial expansions by Muslim rulers across the [[Indian subcontinent]], mainly between the 13th and 18th centuries. Earlier [[Umayyad Caliphate|Umayyad]] campaigns reached India in the 8th century, and [[Mahmud of Ghazni]] invaded Punjab and Gujarat in the 11th century. [[Muhammad of Ghor]] laid the foundations of Muslim rule in India in 1192, and Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji conquered Bengal in 1202. The [[Delhi Sultanate]] was founded in 1206, and under Alauddin Khalji Muslim rule extended to Gujarat, Rajasthan and the Deccan. Timur's invasion in 1398 led to the emergence of several regional sultanates. The Delhi Sultanate was replaced by the [[Mughal Empire]] in 1526. Under [[Akbar]], who stressed religious tolerance, non-Muslim subjects were integrated into the bureaucracy and military. The empire reached its territorial peak under [[Aurangzeb]] at the end of the 17th century and declined after his death in 1707. The conquests halted as the [[East India Company|British East India Company]] took control of much of the subcontinent, and [[British Raj|British rule]] lasted until 1947. Historians disagree over the scale of violence and destruction. The historian K.S. Lal inferred 60–80 million excess deaths among Hindus from 1000 to 1525 CE, and historians debate such estimates.

Arab Muslim [[Hadith|hadith]] scholar, known as Imam Muslim. He was born in Nishapur in the Abbasid province of [[Khorasan]], in what is now northeastern [[Iran]], and was of Arab origin. After studying across the Arabian Peninsula, in [[Egypt]], Iraq and [[Syria]], he settled in Nishapur, where he became a lifelong friend of al-Bukhari. His collection *Sahih Muslim* is one of the six major hadith books of [[Sunni Islam]] and, with *Sahih al-Bukhari*, is considered one of the two most authentic. Muslim's collection shares 2,326 traditions with al-Bukhari's, according to al-Jawzaqi. Estimates of the number of hadiths in it range from three to twelve thousand, depending on whether duplicates are counted. His students included al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Khuzayma.

Adherents of [[Islam]], a monotheistic religion of the Abrahamic tradition. Muslims regard the [[Quran]] as the verbatim word of God as revealed to Muhammad, and most follow the practices attributed to him, known as the sunnah. With an estimated 2 billion followers, Muslims make up around 26% of the world's population. The two largest denominations are [[Sunni Islam|Sunni]] Islam (87–90% of Muslims) and [[Shia Islam|Shia]] Islam (10–13%). [[South Asia]] accounts for the largest share of Muslims (31%). Indonesia is the largest Muslim country, with around 12% of Muslims worldwide, and Pakistan has the second-largest number. Muslims have experienced persecution of varying severity, especially in China, India, parts of Africa and Southeast Asia.

Turkish field marshal and revolutionary statesman, founder of the Republic of Turkey and its first president, 1923–38. Born in [[Thessaloniki|Salonica]] in the [[Ottoman Empire]], he joined opposition movements against Sultan [[Abdul Hamid II]] and took part in the Young Turk Revolution. He rose to prominence in the defense of [[Gallipoli campaign|Gallipoli]] during World War I. After the war he led the Turkish National Movement in the [[Turkish War of Independence]], whose victory was confirmed by the Treaty of Lausanne. His government abolished the sultanate in 1922 and proclaimed the republic in 1923. As president he pursued secularist, Western-oriented reforms, replacing the semi-secular *Mecelle* with a fully secular civil code, introducing a Latin-based alphabet and granting Turkish women equal civil and political rights. Opponents were suppressed, and a one-party regime was established. Supporters praise his military, nation-building and reform record. Critics condemn his dictatorship and assimilationist policies toward minorities such as the Kurds. In 1934 the Turkish Parliament granted him the [[Surname|surname]] Atatürk, meaning "Father of the Turks."

[[Condiment|Condiment]] made by mixing ground mustard seeds with water, vinegar, wine or other liquids, usually with salt and other flavorings. The seeds come from white or yellow mustard (*Sinapis alba*), brown mustard (*Brassica juncea*) or black mustard, all members of the [[Brassicaceae|mustard family]]. The paste ranges in color from bright yellow to dark brown, and in taste from sweet to spicy. Mustard is commonly served with meats, vegetables and cheeses, especially on [[Sandwich|sandwiches]], [[Hamburger|hamburgers]] and [[Hot dog|hot dogs]]. The earliest evidence of human use of mustard as food is a seed cake from the Pre-Pottery Neolithic site of Jerf el Ahmar in Syria, dated to between 9224 and 8753 BC. Yellow mustard paste originated in China during the [[Zhou dynasty]] (1046–256 BC). Dijon, France, had become a recognized center of mustard making by the 13th century, and Dijon mustard was granted an *Appellation d'origine contrôlée* in 1937.

Family of carnivoran mammals that includes [[Weasel|weasels]], [[Badger|badgers]], [[Otter|otters]], [[Sea otter|sea otters]], polecats, martens and [[Wolverine|wolverines]]. The family has between 66 to 70 species in nine subfamilies and is the largest family in the suborder Caniformia. Mustelids vary greatly in size. The least weasel can be under 20 cm (8 in) long, the giant otter of South America can measure up to 1.7 m (5 ft 7 in), and sea otters can exceed 45 kg (99 lb). Most have elongated bodies and short legs, and they are adapted to terrestrial, arboreal or aquatic lives. Most are solitary and nocturnal, and all but the sea otter have anal scent glands. Most mustelids undergo embryonic diapause, which can extend the normal gestation to sometimes up to a year. Only one mustelid, the [[Ferret|ferret]], has been domesticated, while the mink is often raised for its fur. Mustelid-like forms appeared about 40 million years ago.

Shona empire on the northern part of the Zimbabwean Plateau, also called Mwenemutapa or Munhumutapa. The name derives from the Shona royal title Mwene we Mutapa, from *Mwene*, meaning "lord," and *Mutapa*, meaning "conquered land." The plateau is bordered by the [[Zambezi]] and [[Limpopo River|Limpopo]] rivers, the [[Indian Ocean]] and the [[Kalahari Desert]]. Shona oral tradition attributes the demise of [[Great Zimbabwe]] to a salt shortage, and Karanga migrants settled the plateau under an elephant hunter named Mutota. Early-15th-century Angoche traders had opened a route along the Zambezi, and the Karanga increased their power through alliances and succession disputes. Matope, a successor, conquered Tavara and Tonga territory and established his own [[Zimbabwe]] at Bedza. Historians differ on how far these traditions reflect events; one has suggested that Mutota may have been a symbolic figure.

Alteration in the nucleic acid sequence of the genome of an organism, virus or extrachromosomal DNA. Mutations result from errors during [[DNA replication]], [[Mitosis|mitosis]] or [[Meiosis|meiosis]], or from damage to DNA. They may also result from insertion, deletion or substitution of DNA segments by mobile genetic elements. A mutation may or may not change an organism's observable characteristics. Mutations play a part in evolution, cancer and the development of the immune system, and they are the ultimate source of all genetic variation. A 2007 study of *Drosophila* suggested that if a mutation changes a protein, the result is likely to be harmful, with an estimated 70% of amino acid polymorphisms having damaging effects. Unlike DNA damage, which can often be repaired using an undamaged strand as a template, a mutation is a change in the base sequence that is replicated when the cell replicates and is not ordinarily repaired. Causes include [[Ionizing radiation|ionizing radiation]], [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet light]] and chemicals. Germline mutations can be inherited, while somatic mutations contribute to aging and diseases such as cancer. In humans the mutation rate is approximately 1.2 × 10⁻⁸ per base pair per generation.

South Indian Hindu poet, singer, veena player and composer of [[Carnatic music]]. He was the youngest member of the Trinity of Carnatic music, alongside [[Tyagaraja]] and [[Syama Sastri]]. He is credited with around 500 compositions, widely recognized for elaborate poetic descriptions of Hindu deities and detailed depictions of [[Temple|temples]]. His music captures the essence of ragas in the veena style, which highlights gamakas, and his works are usually composed in a slower tempo. Unlike the predominantly Telugu compositions of his contemporaries, most of his works are in [[Sanskrit]], although he also composed a few kritis in Manipravalam, a style combining Sanskrit and Tamil. Born into a Tamil Brahmin family in Tiruvarur, in present-day [[Tamil Nadu]], he was educated by his father in the Vedas, poetry, music and astronomy. He later studied in [[Varanasi]], where he was exposed to [[Hindustani classical music|Hindustani music]]. According to tradition, the deity Murugan at Tiruttani inspired his career and his signature mudra, Guruguha.

Mutiny aboard the [[Royal Navy]] ship *HMS Bounty* in the [[Pacific Ocean]] on April 28, 1789. Disaffected crewmen led by Fletcher Christian seized the ship from its captain, William Bligh, and set him and 18 loyalists adrift in an open launch. The *Bounty* had sailed to collect [[Breadfruit|breadfruit]] plants on [[Tahiti]], and a five-month stay there led many men to be less amenable to naval discipline. The reasons for the mutiny are still debated. Bligh navigated the launch more than 3,500 nautical miles to safety. Christian's group settled on Pitcairn Island, where it remained undiscovered until 1808, when only one mutineer, John Adams, was alive. Descendants of the mutineers and their Tahitian companions have lived on Pitcairn into the 21st century.

American rock band from New Jersey, formed in September 2001. Its current lineup is Gerard Way, Ray Toro, Frank Iero and Mikey Way. The band is considered one of the most influential rock groups of the 2000s and a major act in the [[Emo|emo]] and pop-punk genres, although it rejected the emo label. The 2006 rock opera *The Black Parade* was a major commercial success, and its lead single, "Welcome to the Black Parade," topped the UK singles chart. The band announced its breakup in March 2013 and a reunion in October 2019. Its reunion tour took place in 2022 and ended in early 2023. An untitled fifth studio album is set to begin recording in 2027.
